prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across all five frames, the camera wearer is on a snow-lined sidewalk: the lower sidewalk and nearby snowbanks are brightest and therefore nearest, roughly 0–3 m away, while the road, parked cars, houses, and trees across the street are progressively darker, roughly 8–30+ m away. Foreground tree trunks appear very bright and are about 1–3 m from the camera; they partly occlude the street and houses, shifting from near the left or right edge as the wearer turns and tilts the camera. The map makes the near-to-far layering and the sidewalk’s recession clearer than RGB, but it does not reliably separate similarly distant objects, so distances between the cars and the few distant person-like figures cannot be measured precisely. Bright halos, smoothed boundaries, and inconsistent tones on snow, trees, and the sky make metre estimates approximate, and the changing view looks more like camera rotation and downward tilt than clear approach or retreat.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation identifies several cars across the road, generally about 10–25 m in front of the camera wearer and separated from one another by roughly 3–15 m; some are clipped by the left or right image boundary. In the first frame it also marks several small person instances near the far side of the street, roughly 12–25 m away and far beyond anyone’s arm’s reach, but their tiny masks do not support reliable facing direction, gaze, or person-to-person spacing beyond a rough few metres. Later frames contain only car masks—one or two per view—as the camera turns along and across the sidewalk; the sidewalk, houses, snowbanks, road, and foreground trees remain unlabeled, so their layout must come from RGB. The map helps distinguish small distant instances from the background, but some person masks appear aligned with tree-like or boundary regions and may be false detections, while many obvious scene objects are omitted.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames: it provides no detected body or hand skeletons, no body orientation, no gaze direction, and no arm-reach relationships. Consequently, it cannot confirm the small distant people suggested by the RGB and segmentation maps or determine whether any person faces toward or away from the camera wearer. It also shows no temporal approach, retreat, turning, or articulation across the frames. Its absence of detections is plausibly unreliable here because any people are very small, distant, partly occluded, or poorly resolved; it adds no spatial information beyond indicating that the pose estimator found no usable keypoints.
